gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the ALLWEI 3000W 12V hybrid's '3000W max PV charging power' cannot reach a 12V battery at full rate: 3000 W at 12.8 V works out to about 234 A of charge current. That is more than the 150 A BMS on a typical 12V 100Ah LiFePO4 battery and more than the 100 A charge / 200 A discharge limits of ACOPOWER's own 12V 200Ah battery. Its 3,600 W surge is also only 1.2× its rated output, while ALLWEI's own plain 3000W inverter is rated at 6,000 W peak.
standout_why: I did not open the 12 results ChatGPT got (all renogy.com, none cited). I judged them from their titles and URLs. Most are Renogy solar kits, plus the REGO 3000W inverter charger, a high-frequency inverter charger and a split-phase explainer. None is about the ALLWEI or ACOPOWER all-in-ones ChatGPT recommended, so none could compare these units' PV-charging watts with 12V battery charge-current limits. ChatGPT's own answer lists '3000W output, 12V battery support' and says 'check charging limits' without giving any figures.
decides: This confirms that a 12V all-in-one can't use 3000 W of solar or deliver 3000 W continuously from a single 100–200 Ah battery. For ALLWEI ($599) and ACOPOWER ($1,298), the real limits are the battery's BMS current and the low hybrid surge, not the headline 3000 W. Shoppers who need near-3 kW should take ChatGPT's own advice and move to 24V or 48V. For a 12V unit, the price gap favours ALLWEI only if the loads have modest motor-start surge.
